mechanism: Additive QT-interval prolongation from two or more agents raises torsades de pointes risk; risk is not uniform and depends on each agent's intrinsic TdP potential, dose/route and patient factors.

management.prescriber_action: Weigh whether all QT-prolonging agents are needed; substitute a non-QT alternative for the most dispensable agent where clinically appropriate; if unavoidable, obtain baseline ECG and correct K+/Mg2+.
management.monitoring: Risk factors to weigh: any explicitly contraindicated pair (covered by dedicated rules); presence of a known-TdP-risk agent; route/dose (IV and high dose higher); baseline QTc; hypokalaemia/hypomagnesaemia; bradycardia; heart failure or structural heart disease; renal or hepatic accumulation of a QT agent; older age and female sex; total number of QT agents. Obtain ECG and electrolytes when multiple risk factors coincide.
management.patient_counselling: Seek urgent care for syncope, palpitations, dizziness or blackouts.
management.exceptions: Explicitly contraindicated members (e.g. domperidone + potent CYP3A4 inhibitor or QT drug; ondansetron + apomorphine) are covered by their own contraindication rules and are not merely additive.

mechanism: Clarithromycin and erythromycin prolong the QT interval; added to another QT-prolonging drug the effect is additive. A separate mechanism (clarithromycin/erythromycin CYP3A4 inhibition raising a co-administered CYP3A4-substrate QT drug) is captured by dedicated PK rules.

management.prescriber_action: Prefer a non-QT-prolonging antibiotic where clinically appropriate; do NOT default to azithromycin as QT-safe (lower but non-zero QT risk). If a QT-prolonging macrolide is required, obtain ECG/electrolytes based on patient risk.
management.monitoring: Baseline ECG and K+/Mg2+ where the patient carries additional QT risk factors (see multiple_qt_prolonging_drugs).
management.patient_counselling: Report palpitations, fainting or dizziness; complete the shortest effective antibiotic course.
management.duration: Limit to the shortest effective antibiotic course.
management.exceptions: Clarithromycin/erythromycin CYP3A4 inhibition of specific QT substrates (e.g. domperidone, pimozide) is a separate, sometimes contraindicated, PK interaction.

Do not stop an established antidepressant without prescriber review.

mechanism: Potent CYP3A4 inhibitors raise domperidone plasma concentrations, increasing QT prolongation/torsades risk; the EMA/MHRA review contraindicates this combination.

management.prescriber_action: Do not co-supply — the combination is contraindicated. Clarify with the prescriber: choose an antiemetic/prokinetic without this interaction, or a non-potent-CYP3A4 alternative for the other indication. If domperidone is used, adult dose is 10 mg up to three times daily, max 30 mg/day, shortest duration.
management.monitoring: If the prescriber documents an override, ECG and electrolytes are required (specialist decision).
management.patient_counselling: Report palpitations or fainting; these two medicines must not be taken together.
management.duration: Domperidone: shortest course, typically 1 week or less.
management.exceptions: Domperidone is not FDA-approved in the US; this rule follows EMA/UK/India label context — <verify> jurisdictional wording at promotion.

mechanism: Concomitant ondansetron (5-HT3 antagonist) and apomorphine causes profound hypotension and loss of consciousness — a specific contraindication distinct from QT prolongation.

management.prescriber_action: Do not co-supply — contraindicated. For a patient on apomorphine, choose an antiemetic that is not a 5-HT3 antagonist; do not stop specialist apomorphine therapy, change the antiemetic.
management.patient_counselling: This anti-sickness medicine must not be used with your apomorphine; a severe drop in blood pressure or blackout can occur.
management.exceptions: Class effect — applies to 5-HT3 antagonists generally per apomorphine labelling; both subcutaneous and sublingual apomorphine products carry this contraindication; <verify> exact 5-HT3 member list at promotion.

mechanism: Ondansetron causes dose-dependent QT prolongation (greater with IV and higher single doses); additive with other QT-prolonging drugs.

management.prescriber_action: Use the lowest effective ondansetron dose; avoid the 32 mg single IV dose; correct electrolytes; consider a non-QT antiemetic where risk factors coincide.
management.monitoring: ECG and K+/Mg2+ with additional QT risk factors; the IV route warrants closer attention.
management.exceptions: Ondansetron + apomorphine is a separate contraindication (hypotension/LOC), not this additive-QT rule.

mechanism: Parenteral (especially IV) and high-dose haloperidol carry a higher QT/torsades risk (subject of an FDA warning); additive with other QT-prolonging drugs.

management.prescriber_action: IV haloperidol is not an FDA-approved route and requires continuous ECG monitoring if used; use the lowest dose; avoid stacking QT-prolonging drugs; prefer the oral route where clinically appropriate.
management.monitoring: Continuous or serial ECG and electrolytes when IV or high-dose haloperidol is combined with another QT drug.
management.patient_counselling: Administered/monitored in a clinical setting; report palpitations.
management.exceptions: Oral maintenance haloperidol carries lower (non-zero) risk — see haloperidol_oral__qt_prolonging_drug.

mechanism: Ziprasidone produces greater QT prolongation than several other antipsychotics; additive with other QT-prolonging drugs.

management.prescriber_action: Generally avoid combining ziprasidone with other QT-prolonging drugs; assess baseline QTc, electrolytes and other risk factors before any addition. Do not stop established antipsychotic therapy without prescriber review.

mechanism: Methadone causes dose-dependent QT prolongation; additive with other QT-prolonging drugs. A separate PK mechanism (CYP inhibition raising methadone) is captured by methadone__cyp_inhibitor.

management.prescriber_action: Do not withhold established methadone (opioid substitution therapy or analgesia); confirm the added QT drug is necessary, prefer a non-QT alternative, and arrange ECG based on methadone dose, baseline QTc and risk factors.
management.monitoring: ECG stratified by methadone dose and baseline QTc; correct K+/Mg2+.
management.patient_counselling: Do not stop methadone; report palpitations or fainting; attend for ECG if arranged.
management.exceptions: Established specialist opioid substitution therapy must not be unilaterally stopped by the pharmacist.

mechanism: CYP3A4/2B6/2D6 inhibitors reduce methadone clearance, raising plasma concentration and QT/torsades and opioid-toxicity risk. Not all CYP inhibitors are equivalent — the relevant isoenzyme and inhibitor strength determine the effect.

management.prescriber_action: Do not withhold established methadone; assess the specific inhibitor (isoenzyme and strength); watch for sedation/opioid toxicity and QT; adjust methadone only under prescriber direction with ECG where indicated.
management.monitoring: Opioid-toxicity signs and ECG per methadone dose/baseline QTc when a relevant CYP inhibitor is added or stopped (stopping an inhibitor can precipitate withdrawal).
management.patient_counselling: Do not stop methadone; report drowsiness, slow breathing or palpitations.
management.exceptions: The perpetrator set is scoped to methadone-relevant CYP inhibitors (principally CYP3A4 and CYP2B6, minor CYP2D6) — it is NOT a mechanical expansion of all CYP inhibitors; <verify> the curated member list and per-isoenzyme strength at promotion. Enzyme inducers have the opposite effect (reduced methadone, withdrawal/loss of efficacy) — a separate rule.

mechanism: Hydroxychloroquine prolongs QT; combined with another QT-prolonging drug the additive risk depends on baseline QT, electrolytes, bradycardia, structural heart disease, renal/hepatic accumulation and the second agent's TdP potential.

management.prescriber_action: Assess overall QT risk rather than applying blanket avoidance; correct electrolytes; where the second agent has high TdP potential or risk factors coincide, obtain ECG or choose a non-QT alternative. Do not stop established HCQ (e.g. for lupus or RA) without prescriber review.
management.monitoring: Baseline ECG and K+/Mg2+ when risk factors coincide or the second agent is a known-TdP-risk drug.
management.exceptions: HCQ plus a single low-risk QT agent in a low-risk patient may be acceptable with counselling.
